title: Long Distance Relationship Advice: 15 Tips That Work
h1: Long Distance Relationship Advice: 15 Tips to Stay Close (and Make It Last)
description: Practical long distance relationship advice: how to communicate without pressure, build trust, plan visits, keep romance alive and close the gap.
excerpt: Miles apart but still in love? Fifteen practical tips for communication, trust, visits and romance — plus how to plan the day you finally close the gap.
intro:
Long distance relationships get a bad reputation, but plenty of couples not only survive the miles — they come out stronger. Distance forces you to talk more intentionally, trust more deliberately and appreciate time together in a way that couples who see each other every day can take for granted.

It's also genuinely hard. Time zones, missed moments, loneliness and the occasional jealous spiral can wear on even the most committed couple. This long distance relationship advice focuses on what actually helps: setting expectations early, communicating without turning it into an obligation, building trust, keeping romance alive from afar and, most importantly, having a shared plan to eventually be in the same place.
body:
Start with an honest conversation about expectations

1. Agree on what you are

Before anything else, make sure you're on the same page about commitment. Are you exclusive? How do you each feel about the distance? Assumptions cause most early long distance heartbreak, so say it out loud.

2. Talk about how often you'll communicate

Some couples love a daily video call; others prefer texting through the day and a longer call on weekends. There's no right answer, but mismatched expectations can quickly lead to hurt feelings. Discuss what feels good to each of you and adjust as you go.

3. Discuss what trust looks like

What are you each comfortable with when it comes to going out, friendships and social media? Agreeing on boundaries early prevents a lot of anxiety later. Boundaries should feel mutual and reasonable, not like one person monitoring the other.

Communicate without making it a chore

4. Keep communication natural, not mandatory

Talking every day can be lovely, but turning it into a rigid requirement can make it feel like a job. If one of you is exhausted or busy, a quick “Thinking of you, talk tomorrow” should be enough. Quality matters more than quantity. A relaxed 20-minute call where you're both present beats an hour of distracted scrolling while on the phone.

5. Share the boring stuff

Long distance couples often save conversations for big news, but closeness lives in the small details. Send a photo of your lunch, a voice note on your commute, a complaint about your coworker's microwave fish. These little updates help you feel part of each other's daily lives.

6. Be slow to judge

Text messages lose tone, and time zones mean replies can be delayed for perfectly innocent reasons. Before assuming the worst about a short reply or a missed call, give your partner the benefit of the doubt and ask calmly. Our guide on how to deal with jealousy can help when worry creeps in.

7. Talk about hard things on video, not text

Disagreements are much easier to resolve when you can see each other's faces and hear each other's voices. If a conversation over text starts getting tense, suggest a call. Avoid going to bed angry when you can't physically reconnect the next morning.

Tip: Set up a shared calendar showing both time zones, work schedules and visit dates. It removes guesswork and makes planning calls much easier.

Big time-zone differences need extra creativity. If one of you is waking up as the other goes to bed, find a reliable overlap — maybe a weekend breakfast call for one person that's a Saturday-night chat for the other. Asynchronous connection helps too: record a short video before bed for your partner to watch with their morning coffee, or keep a shared note or photo album you both add to throughout the day. These habits let you feel present in each other's lives even when you can't talk in real time. And on the hard days, remember that a missed call isn't a missed relationship. What matters is the overall pattern of effort and care you both bring.

Keep the romance alive from afar

8. Have virtual dates

Cook the same recipe together over video, watch a movie in sync, play an online game, take a virtual museum tour or simply eat dinner “together.” Put the same effort into a virtual date as an in-person one — dress up, plan ahead, put your phone on do-not-disturb.

9. Send something physical

A handwritten letter, a care package, a hoodie that smells like you or a surprise food delivery makes the distance feel smaller. Physical reminders matter because they give your partner something to hold. Need words for the letter? Browse our I love you letters.

10. Learn each other's love language

Some people feel most loved through words, others through gifts, time, acts of service or touch. Touch is tricky at a distance, so get creative: long, attentive calls for quality time, thoughtful messages for words of affirmation, helping with a task remotely for acts of service. Our guide on how to show love has more ideas.

11. Keep intimacy respectful and mutual

Flirting and affection keep the spark alive. If you share intimate messages or photos, make sure it's something you're both fully comfortable with, never pressure each other and consider privacy carefully before sending anything you wouldn't want saved.

Make visits count

12. Always have the next visit on the calendar

Having a date to look forward to is one of the most powerful things a long distance couple can do. Even if it's months away, a countdown turns “I miss you” into “I'll see you soon.” Try to book the next visit before the current one ends.

13. Balance adventure and ordinary life

It's tempting to pack every visit with special plans, but you also need to see how you function in everyday life — grocery runs, lazy mornings, meeting each other's friends. That ordinary time is valuable information for a future together.

14. Plan for the post-visit slump

Saying goodbye after a visit can hit hard. Expect a dip in mood, plan something comforting for the day after and schedule a call soon after you part. Talking about the next visit right away softens the blow.

Make sure the gap is temporary

15. Build a shared plan to close the distance

This is the most important piece of long distance relationship advice: the distance needs an end date, even a rough one. Without a plan to eventually live in the same place, a relationship can drift into a holding pattern. Talk honestly about:

  • Who might move, and what that would mean for each person's career, family and friends
  • A realistic timeline, such as after graduation, a contract ending or a savings goal
  • Practical steps like job searching, visa research or apartment hunting
  • How you'll handle it if plans need to change

You don't need every detail sorted. But you both need to be moving toward the same destination.

Take care of yourself while you're apart

Your partner shouldn't be your only source of happiness, especially when they're far away. Keep up your friendships, hobbies, exercise and goals. A full life makes you a more interesting partner, gives you plenty to talk about and keeps loneliness from turning into resentment. If loneliness is hitting hard, read how to deal with loneliness.

Signs your long distance relationship is struggling

Every couple has rough patches, but watch for these patterns:

  • One person is always the one reaching out or planning visits.
  • Conversations feel like obligations rather than something you look forward to.
  • There's no agreement or effort toward closing the gap.
  • Trust issues keep resurfacing despite reassurance.
  • You feel lonelier in the relationship than you would outside it.

If several of these sound familiar, have an honest conversation about what each of you needs. Sometimes recommitting with a clearer plan revives things. Sometimes it's a sign the relationship has run its course.

The bottom line

Long distance can be one of the most meaningful tests a relationship ever goes through. Set clear expectations, keep communication warm rather than mandatory, be slow to judge, stay creative with romance and always have something to look forward to. Above all, make sure you're both working toward closing the gap. With commitment and a shared plan, the miles can become part of your story rather than the end of it.
takeaways: Agree early on commitment, communication rhythm and trust boundaries.
Quality, relaxed communication beats mandatory daily check-ins.
Virtual dates, letters and care packages keep romance alive.
Always have the next visit on the calendar to look forward to.
A shared plan to close the gap is the most important ingredient.

faq.q: Can long distance relationships really work?
faq.a: Yes, many do, especially when both people are committed, communicate honestly, trust each other and share a realistic plan to eventually live in the same place. Long distance often struggles when there is no end date or when one partner is far more invested than the other.

faq.q: How often should you talk in a long distance relationship?
faq.a: There is no perfect number. Some couples talk daily, others connect a few times a week. What matters is that both partners feel satisfied and that communication feels natural rather than obligatory. Discuss your needs openly and adjust as schedules and feelings change.

faq.q: How do you keep a long distance relationship exciting?
faq.a: Plan virtual dates like cooking the same meal or watching a movie together, send surprise letters or care packages, share small everyday moments through photos and voice notes and always keep the next visit on the calendar so you have something to look forward to.

faq.q: How long can a long distance relationship last?
faq.a: It can last as long as both people are committed and moving toward a shared plan. Couples often find the distance easier when there is a clear end date, even if it is a year or more away. Open-ended distance without a plan tends to be harder to sustain.
